sources.title: Anthropic lifts Nasdaq futures and tech stocks ahead of its record-breaking IPO
sources.text: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk. A historic IPO for markets and an exclusive for CNBC. Andrew Ross Sorkin will speak to Anthropic co-Founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei at 10 a.m. ET, as the biggest public listing in history starts trading on the Nasdaq. Anthropic has priced its IPO above the expected range, at $83 per share . With around 980 million shares sold, it has raised $81.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX's record IPO back in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq today under the ticker symbol "ANT." CNBC's Leslie Picker will report from the Nasdaq throughout the trading day. Nasdaq futures are higher in anticipation, as traders gear up for this historic moment. Shares in chipmakers and companies that are invested in Anthropic are also higher premarket. Shares in Nvidia are gaining in premarket trading, alongside other tech heavyweights Amazon , Alphabet and Broadcom . Palo Alto shares are jumping over 9% in premarket trading, after the group raised its annual revenue forecast. The move is also pulling cybersecurity shares higher too. An unprecedented trilateral summit has taken place between U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. In Shenzhen, China, each leader spoke about the importance of their "special responsibility" to ensure global peace. Here are some key quotes: CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning. It's the most anticipated video game in a generation. After 13 long years, gamers can finally play "Grand Theft Auto VI" as its global rollout gets underway. It's not just players rejoicing; investors are also applauding the blockbuster release. Shares in the studio behind the game, Take-Two Interactive , traded higher on the revenue boost. Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access After a string of outages disrupted airlines , banks and even the National Security Agency , U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen. The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash , a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person . — CNBC's Ashley Capoot, Leslie Picker, Greg Iacurci, Julia Boorstin, Luke Fountain, and Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
sources.text: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since . For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures , shifting priorities , and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks. Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring , while operating losses are declining . Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures. Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.) Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries . Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives. Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there. Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit. At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says.

sources.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
sources.text: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. stories.title: Maior IPO da história: Anthropic supera desconfiança com IA e vale mais que a SpaceX, de Ellon Musk
stories.summary: Criadora do Claude captou US$ 107 bilhões, superando os US$ 75 bilhões da SpaceX. Avaliada em US$ 1,5 trilhão, empresa atrai investidores com forte crescimento, mas enfrenta custos bilionários para sustentar a expansão.

sources.name: Convergencia Digital
sources.title: Maior IPO da história: Anthropic supera desconfiança com IA e vale mais que a SpaceX, de Ellon Musk
sources.text: Em um momento que a Inteligência Artificial está sob críticas – até por conta dos ataques hackers originados com o uso da tecnologia – os investidores cravam que a demanda por ferramentas de inteligência artificial continuará crescendo, à medida que empresas de diferentes setores ampliem o uso desses serviços. E o resultado é que a Anthropic, dona do Claude, faz nesta quinta-feira (19) a maior estreia de uma empresa na bolsa de valores da história. A criadora do Claude movimentou US$ 107 bilhões (R$ 629 bilhões) com a venda de ações, superando os US$ 85,7 bilhões (R$ 504,1 bilhões) captados pela SpaceX em junho. A empresa arrecadou US$ 81,3 bilhões (R$ 478,3 bilhões) com a venda de 980 milhões de ações, a um preço médio de US$ 83 (R$ 488) por papel. Além disso, levantou outros US$ 26 bilhões com a venda de ações para grandes investidores, como Google, Nvidia e AMD. Além do valor captado, a estreia chama a atenção pela avaliação de US$ 1,5 trilhão (R$ 8,8 trilhões) atribuída à companhia. Esse cálculo representa o valor de mercado estimado da empresa como um todo, e não apenas os recursos que entrarão em seu caixa com a venda de ações. Segundo dados apresentados à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC, na sigla em inglês), a empresa registrou faturamento de US$ 33,2 bilhões (cerca de R$ 194,55 bilhões) nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, mais de sete vezes o valor de US$ 4,585 bilhões (R$ 26,87 bilhões) registrado em todo o ano de 2025. Esse crescimento também aparece no número de clientes corporativos. No fim de setembro, mais de 11,9 mil empresas haviam gerado, cada uma, pelo menos US$ 100 mil (R$ 586 mil) em receita para a Anthropic nos 12 meses anteriores. Cerca de 250 delas haviam superado US$ 10 milhões (R$ 58,6 milhões) em receita no mesmo período. O aval foi dado, mas especialistas afirmam que um dos principais desafios da Anthropic é o custo de acompanhar o crescimento da inteligência artificial. Desenvolver modelos mais avançados e atender a um número cada vez maior de usuários exige investimentos contínuos em computadores, data centers e infraestrutura.

sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Anthropic levanta US$ 81 bi no maior IPO da história e supera SpaceX
sources.text: Por Marcelo Fischer | 19/11/2026 às 17:03 A Anthropic, empresa responsável pela inteligência artificial (IA) Claude, estreou na bolsa de valores dos Estados Unidos nesta quinta-feira (19) após levantar US$ 81,3 bilhões (cerca de R$ 481,5 bilhões) na maior oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO) da história. Os papéis abriram em alta de 34%, levando a companhia a atingir um valor de mercado estimado em US$ 2 trilhões . A empresa iniciou as negociações na Nasdaq, bolsa de tecnologia de Nova York, sob o código ANT. Cada ação foi vendida inicialmente por US$ 83, mas começou a ser negociada a US$ 111,50, segundo a Reuters. Com o resultado, a Anthropic superou o recorde estabelecido pela SpaceX, de Elon Musk, em junho deste ano, e se tornou a primeira das principais desenvolvedoras de modelos avançados de IA a abrir seu capital. A valorização inicial, entretanto, perdeu força ao longo do dia. No início da tarde, as ações eram negociadas abaixo dos US$ 100, enquanto as bolsas americanas registravam perdas em meio às preocupações dos investidores com os altos custos da inteligência artificial. O IPO é o processo pelo qual uma empresa passa a negociar suas ações publicamente pela primeira vez, permitindo que investidores comprem participações em seu negócio. No caso da Anthropic, foram ofertadas 980 milhões de ações a US$ 83 cada , valor superior à faixa inicialmente prevista de US$ 70 a US$ 78. O preço estabelecido na operação avaliou a companhia em aproximadamente US$ 1,5 trilhão, considerando também ações que poderão ser emitidas futuramente. Segundo o comunicado oficial, cerca de 956,4 milhões de ações foram vendidas pela própria Anthropic. As outras 23,6 milhões pertenciam a acionistas que aproveitaram a operação para negociar parte de suas participações. A empresa também autorizou os bancos responsáveis pela oferta a vender até 147 milhões de ações adicionais, o que poderá elevar o valor total do IPO para aproximadamente US$ 93,5 bilhões. Paralelamente, a Anthropic recebeu US$ 26 bilhões em uma colocação privada de ações, com a participação de empresas como Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD e Broadcom, segundo a Reuters. Somando as duas operações, o volume de recursos negociados ultrapassa US$ 107 bilhões. Parte desse dinheiro, porém, corresponde à venda de participações por acionistas existentes e não entra diretamente no caixa da Anthropic. A estreia da Anthropic foi acompanhada de forte volatilidade nas bolsas americanas. Depois de abrir a US$ 111,50 e superar momentaneamente os US$ 115, a ação perdeu parte dos ganhos e chegou à faixa dos US$ 97 no início da tarde. Mesmo após o recuo, os papéis permaneciam cerca de 17% acima do preço definido no IPO. O resultado demonstra o interesse dos investidores pela empresa, mas também evidencia as oscilações que podem ocorrer no primeiro dia de negociação. A movimentação aconteceu em um dia de perdas para os principais índices de Wall Street. Por volta das 12h45, no horário de Nova York, o S&P 500 caía 1,1%, enquanto o Nasdaq recuava 1% e o Dow Jones perdia 1,5%, segundo a Associated Press. Na Europa, as bolsas também fecharam em baixa. De acordo com a CNN Brasil, o índice FTSE 100, de Londres, caiu 0,93%, enquanto o DAX, da Alemanha, recuou 0,92%, e o CAC 40, da França, perdeu 0,81%. A queda dos mercados europeus também foi influenciada por tensões geopolíticas no Oriente Médio e pela guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia. Algumas empresas ligadas à fabricação de semicondutores, entretanto, registraram ganhos. A holandesa ASML avançou 2,2%, enquanto a ASM International subiu 3,1%. Fundada em 2021 pelos irmãos Dario e Daniela Amodei e outros ex-funcionários da OpenAI, a Anthropic cresceu principalmente com a comercialização dos modelos Claude e de ferramentas como o Claude Code, voltado à programação. A empresa registrou uma receita de US$ 16,96 bilhões no terceiro trimestre de 2026 , crescimento de 47% em relação aos três meses anteriores. Ao final de outubro, a receita anualizada, calculada a partir do ritmo recente de vendas, havia chegado a US$ 81 bilhões. Os investimentos necessários para sustentar esse crescimento também aumentaram. Segundo documentos apresentados pela Anthropic, a companhia gastou aproximadamente US$ 9 bilhões com infraestrutura e capacidade computacional apenas no primeiro semestre de 2026. No terceiro trimestre, a empresa registrou prejuízo operacional de US$ 567 milhões. O prejuízo líquido foi de US$ 23,3 bilhões, influenciado por ajustes contábeis relacionados a títulos conversíveis em ações. Esses números ajudam a explicar por que o IPO é acompanhado de perto por investidores e analistas. Há dúvidas sobre a capacidade das empresas de inteligência artificial de transformar os investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura em lucros sustentáveis. A estreia também coloca pressão sobre a OpenAI, principal concorrente da Anthropic e responsável pelo ChatGPT. A expectativa é que a companhia avance com seus próprios planos de abertura de capital em 2027. O IPO ocorre após um período de preocupação com a possibilidade de uma bolha no setor. Em outubro, o Canaltech mostrou que a avaliação pretendida pela Anthropic havia sofrido um corte de US$ 500 bilhões durante as negociações com investidores. Veja também: Afinal, o que é IPO? sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
sources.text: With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows. With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows. Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says . Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale. Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US. Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta .

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Google Gemini can now perform agentic tasks on your Mac
sources.text: You can hand over control to Gemini if you really want to No longer is Gemini a passive Mac app that simply sits on the sidebar. Google has introduced a new “@Computer use” command in the Gemini for Mac app , allowing Gemini to access files, edit documents, run apps, and even access the internet. But as with all AI with agentic capabilities, you might not want to give it total access to your precious family photos or important files because it can make mistakes. Luckily, Google has planned ahead with a key feature that’ll prevent Gemini from completely wiping your Mac. Google’s announcement showcases that with a simple prompt, Gemini could take a child’s sketch of a butterfly and turn it into a fully rigged model in Blender, create an alternative reality app that allows the butterfly to fly around the room, and even turn the drawing into a design for a 3D printed ring. Outside of the fun ways to use it, Gemini can take over mundane tasks such as tidying up folders, batch-processing forms and images, or putting together a presentation or slideshow from local files. Rather than taking over your mouse and keyboard to run its errands, Gemini will instead type, click buttons, and navigate in a background window, allowing you to continue using your device without being interrupted. For those worried about Gemini modifying or deleting something important, Google has got you covered. You have granular control over what Gemini can and cannot access, and Gemini will create temporary backup copies of every file it interacts with. These files are either deleted once you start a new task — provided you’re happy with the outcome — or automatically removed after 24 hours. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Google is slightly late to adding system-level computer control to its Mac app, given that Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic already offer similar features. The feature is only available on Macs with Apple Silicon, such as newer MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, Mac mini, and iMac models, running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later. Sorry, free users, this feature is paid-plan only, requiring a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. It's also currently restricted to users aged 18 or older in the US, and only works in English. stories.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
stories.summary: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
sources.text: It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life. Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days. The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues. Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more. While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly. Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related. The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch. The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said. This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said. Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X . AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with. In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up. When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.” Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said. Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.” Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues. And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said. “There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . sources.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
sources.text: Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services. Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services. Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a now-removed job listing spotted by Bloomberg , which said Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant. An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse , OpenAI’s Dots , Anthropic’s Duet , and Google’s Tasks . Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same. Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities , as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions. “People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing said. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.” With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update , Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps. Update, November 20th: Added that the job listing has since been removed.

sources.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
sources.text: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things. The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.” “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.” TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response. Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit. Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers. The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . sources.title: Here’s who’s getting the richest from Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO
sources.text: Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the company’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich. Dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes. These commitments, though, are voluntary and not legally binding, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing. The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic announced that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion. After pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the company opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat , the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart . The record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the most. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic’s president and chair of the board, Daniela Amodei, are among the figures most commonly associated with the company. But there are another five cofounders who are cashing in as well. Each of its seven cofounders owns between 237 million and 241 million shares after the offering. At the stock’s price of about $85 on Friday, that means each founder has holdings worth approximately $20 billion, putting them (at least on paper) in the same league as Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who has a net worth of $21 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Each founder also sold approximately 3.38 million shares in the IPO, worth about $280 million at the offering price. Despite owning a minority of the company’s equity, Anthropic’s cofounders control 50.1% of its shareholder voting power. The nearly equal distribution of shares among the seven founders is unusual for a Silicon Valley startup, Fortune reported . Besides its cofounders, some Silicon Valley investors are also set to win big. Lightspeed Venture Partners, an early backer of Snapchat, led a $3.5 billion funding round in Anthropic in March 2025 when the company was valued at $61.5 billion. The VC firm owns less than 2% of the company, according to Bloomberg , yet its stake is still reportedly worth tens of billions of dollars. Other VCs like Menlo Ventures also own a stake representing less than 2% of the company, Bloomberg reported. Iconiq has invested more than $6 billion in Anthropic since 2025, and its stake is worth more than $26 billion, the outlet reported. Anthropic in total has more than 400 venture investors, according to PitchBook, yet no VC firm owns more than 5%, Fortune reported . The company’s historic IPO means even some smaller stakes are now worth billions. Sound Ventures, the venture firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher, invested about $435 million in Anthropic and owns about 0.5% of the company , Bloomberg reported. It’s unclear, though, how much Kutcher himself benefited from the trade as the actor best known for his role on That ’70s Show stepped down as general partner at the firm earlier this year. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also owns about 1% of Anthropic , according to Bloomberg , putting his stake’s value at about $11 billion at Friday’s share price. One early investor who won’t be reaping the rewards is FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is serving a sentence of 25 years in prison after being convicted on fraud and conspiracy charges. Bankman-Fried has appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court. The trading firm he founded, Alameda Research, invested $500 million in Anthropic, but FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold most of its stake in 2024 to repay creditors. Among the buyers was Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street, which stands to reap a multibillion-dollar windfall . Many of the company’s roughly 5,300 employees are also getting rich thanks to generous stock-based compensation. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimated that 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity in the company at a $1.35 trillion valuation, Reuters reported . Some of the earliest employees stand to benefit disproportionately. At least 400 early hires could hold equity worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC. To be sure, it’s hard to estimate which employees hold how much stock because Anthropic’s IPO filing discloses aggregate equity awards but not their distribution among individual employees. Now that Anthropic is public, non-founder employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of certain holdings, and up to another 35% following the release of Anthropic’s 2026 financial results. Some of the biggest gains from the company’s IPO will go to two Big Tech giants, Amazon and Google. Anthropic’s IPO filing estimated that Amazon would own 14.6% of the company’s outstanding shares and Google would own 13.4%. Amazon’s stake stems from billions of dollars in investments the company has made in Anthropic dating back to 2023, around the time it had just 160 employees. At the time, Amazon committed an initial $1.25 billion as part of a deal to ultimately invest $4 billion in Anthropic. In exchange Anthropic agreed to make Amazon Web Services its primary cloud provider for critical workloads and make Claude available to AWS customers. In total, Amazon inv
